questions.q: What does d mean in ARIMA(p,d,q)?
options: The number of times the series is differenced
why: Correct: d is the degree of differencing.
That is p.
Seasons belong to SARIMA.
Errors are not part of the order.

questions.q: Which ARIMA model is a random walk?
why: Correct: no AR, no MA, one difference: y(t) = y(t-1) + e(t).
That is AR(1).
That is MA(1).
That has AR and MA parts on top of the difference.

For an MA(2) model, what is the forecast for h = 3 (beyond q)?
why: Correct: after q steps no known shock remains, so the forecast is the mean.
That is the naive forecast.
Only if the mean is zero.
The last shock only has an effect up to q steps.

questions.q: Last value 200. The ARIMA(p,1,q) model forecasts differences 5, 4, 3. What is the level forecast for h = 3?
Is an MA(1) with theta = -0.8 invertible?
why: Correct: only the absolute size matters. The root is z = 1/0.8 = 1.25, outside the unit circle.
The sign does not decide invertibility.
Being below 1 in absolute value is the requirement.
It can be computed from theta.

questions.q: A colleague fits ARIMA(5,2,5) to a monthly sales series with 40 points because it has the lowest training error. What is the problem?
options: Too many parameters for 40 points: overfitting. Compare small models with AIC and a backtest
Nothing, lowest training error is best
ARIMA cannot be used on monthly data
why: Correct: 10 parameters and two differences on 40 points will fit the noise.
Training error always falls with more parameters, so it is a poor guide.
d = 2 is allowed but rare, and should be justified.
ARIMA works on any regular frequency.
